task.title: Let's isolate the Staging and Production Environments !!
task.content:
Summary

Your organization has recently decided to adopt serverless architectures to build its next generation of service APIs. The development teams have been using AWS API Gateway and AWS Lambda to build powerful APIs to their customers. However, developers have been using a single environment to build and test the APIs and now need your help to build fully isolated environments for testing (staging) and production purposes. They know it is important to separate these environments so that they can continue to improve the APIs without affecting customers using a stable version of the APIs in production.

You were tasked to create a blue/green deployment model that could serve as basis for deploying the various service APIs currently being developed within your organization. The blue/green model must enforce the full isolation of the "staging" (green) and the "production" (blue) environments.

You have no time to waste! So, you started by creating a very simple API called Greeting API that will help you build and test your model. Then, you created two API Gateway stages (staging and prod), a Lambda function (GreetingLambda) that implements the API logic, and two Lambda aliases (staging and prod). Your plan is to have the "staging" API endpoint resolve to the "staging" Lambda alias and the "prod" API stage resolve to the "prod" Lambda alias. This way new changes made to the Lambda code can be deployed to the "staging" alias first and be visible only from the "staging" API endpoint. When you're ready to push the changes to production you can simply update the "prod" Lambda alias to point to the same Lambda version referenced by the "staging" alias. Things look great and you're confident that you have all the pieces in place (ie, two API stages and two Lambda aliases).

But, wait... When you hit the production and staging API endpoints from your web browser you always get the same results back even if new changes were deployed only to the staging environment. Hmmm, that's intriguing... You now have to dive deep and figure out what configuration is missing to fully isolate the production and staging environments.

Important Parameters

Take note of the following stack outputs (under Output Properties):

  • APIStagingStageGreetingURL: URL of the staging (Green) API environment
  • APIProdStageGreetingURL: URL of the production (Blue) API environment
  • CheckChallengeAnswerURL: URL that will give the answer to this challenge once you solve it

Solving this Challenge

First things first... So, let's start troubleshooting the problem. Your first goal will be to make a small change to the Lambda code and deploy it as a new version into the "staging" environment only. Follow the steps below.

Step #1: Make a small change to the Lambda function code

Open the AWS Lambda Console and click on your Lambda function: GreetingLambda. You should now see the Lambda editor. Use the editor to replace the greeting string from "Hello" to "Hi", in the source code. Hit "Deploy", wait for the deployment to complete then hit Test" to test your Lambda changes. The console might ask you to create a test event. If so, use the "Hello World" test event as a reference. Enter an event name (eg, "GreetingTestEvent") and in the event template type this JSON input: {"name": "awsstudent"} (delete the default event template: {"key3": "value3", ...}). Hit "Create" to create the test event. Click on "Test" to run the Lambda function. Now, expand the "Execution result" panel by clicking on "details" to see the output logs of the Lambda execution. Did you notice that now the function greets you with {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"}?

Now that you have made a change to the Lambda code you will deploy it into the "staging" environment. This is accomplished by publishing a new version of the Lambda code and updating the "staging" alias to point to that new version. Follow step #2 below.

Step #2: Publish a new version of the Lambda function code and deploy it to the "staging" environment.

Still on the Lambda Console, click on "Versions" and then "Publish new version". Use a simple version description like "version 2". Note that you are only able to publish a new version of the Lambda function because you have changed the Lambda code. If you go back to the Lambda function main screen and click on "Versions" you should be able to see multiple versions of your Lambda function now. You will also notice that the two Lambda aliases (staging and prod) refer to version 1. Let's update the staging alias to point to version 2, the version that contains the code changes you made in the previous step. Back in the Lambda function main screen, click on "Aliases". Select the staging alias by clicking on the corresponding radio button then hit the "Edit" button. Update the Lambda version in the staging alias to version 2 and hit "Save". Now click on the alias name (should be a clickable link) and hit "Test" to run the Lambda function. Expand the Lambda execution logs panel again by hitting "Execution results", at the top of the page, and then "details". Did you notice that now the staging alias returns {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"}? Now do the same procedure but selecting the prod alias and notice that the output produced is different: {"greeting": "Hello, awsstudent!"}, as expected! That's great. This means that your changes only affected the staging environment.

So, the Lambda aliases are working just fine and you are able to deploy changes to the "staging" alias without affecting the "prod" alias. Your next step will be to troubleshoot the API Gateway configuration.

Step #3: Troubleshoot the API Gateway configuration.

Open your web browser, hit the staging and production API endpoints again (find the URLs from Output Properties APIStagingStageGreetingURL and APIProdStageGreetingURL). What do you see? Both endpoints return {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"}? But, why? Why do both endpoints now return "Hi" if you only updated the "staging" Lambda alias in steps #1 and #2?

Since you have tested your Lambda aliases and they are working just fine the issue must be an API Gateway misconfiguration. Congrats, you have narrow down the issue. Most of your troubleshooting work will now take place in the API Gateway Console!

Now, to the real deal! Your tasks in this challenge are:

  • To troubleshoot the API misconfiguration and figure out why both API endpoints ("staging" and "prod") return the same results despite the fact that you only updated the staging Lambda alias
  • To fix the issue so that these API endpoints return the expected results (eg, {"greeting": "Hi, awsstudent!"} for staging (reflecting your changes to the Lambda code) and {"greeting": "Hello, awsstudent!"} for prod)

How do I know that I've solved this challenge?

Open a web browser and visit the URL indicated in the Output Property CheckChallengeAnswerURL. The answer to this challenge will be revealed to you once you have solved the challenge.

Good luck!

task.title: Call Amazon Bedrock from AWS Lambda
task.content:
## Background:
AnyTaxCity was able to find a sample chatbot application online which they set up in their AWS account. 
This chatbot uses a simple html front-end in Amazon S3, which is put behind a Amazon CloudFront Distribution. 

For the backend  of this application the sample chatbot uses an Amazon API gateway which sends the requests to an AWS Lambda function. This AWS Lambda function takes the user input and sends the request to the *Amazon Nova Lite* Model in Amazon Bedrock and responds with the generated output.

## Your Task

This sample chatbot uses the knowledge of the pretrained model to respond to questions. Adjust the Lambda function (*GenAI-chatbot-backend-LambdaFunction*) to use [retrieval augmented generation with Amazon Bedrock](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/1.35.8/reference/services/bedrock-agent-runtime/client/retrieve_and_generate.html). Also, make sure you enable model access to the *Nova Lite* model in the account.

You can test this sample application using the Amazon Cloudfront distribution link in the output parameters of the JAM platform.

## Inventory
The following resources have been pre-created for this challenge:
- AWS Lambda function to process requests to the chatbot.
- Amazon S3 bucket with front-end code.
- Amazon CloudFront distribution to server the front-end. 
- Amazon API Gateway to send the API's from the front-end to.
- Knowledge base for Amazon Bedrock, which was created in the previous task.



## Services you should use
- AWS Lambda
- Amazon Bedrock (SDK)

## Validation
Once you have successfully set up the Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock and changed the AWS Lambda code to call the *RetrieveAndGenerate* API, you can test your chatbot via the Amazon CloudFront URL provided in the output parameters.

To validate the code, ask the chatbot the following question: "What is the flat income tax rate of AnyTaxCity?". The numeric answer to this question is the answer you need to put into the textbox. 


### Factors that must be true for the task to be successful: 
- After you created the Knowledge base, you will need to 'sync' the data source you set up to ensure the Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock gets populated. Make sure you enabled the correct Amazon Bedrock models to do this.
- Change the AWS Lambda function (*GenAI-chatbot-backend-LambdaFunction*) to perform RAG using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock

## Important Information

You are using a training account with limited access to Amazon Bedrock. Due to the service quotas set for Requests per Minute (RPM), Tokens per Minute (TPM) and Tokens per Day (TPD) , you may encounter throttling issues. To mitigate these issues:

    Execute code blocks one at a time. If you receive an error, wait a few seconds before retrying.
    Avoid running multiple operations concurrently.
    If throttling persists, wait 2 minutes before running any code that interacts with Bedrock.
    If the problem continues after waiting, you may need to end the lab and start again.

We understand this is not ideal and are working hard to implement a permanent solution. Following these steps will help ensure a smoother experience as you explore Amazon Bedrock’s capabilities. In the interim, please provide the details of any problems you encounter using the https://support.aws.amazon.com/#/contacts/aws-training.

task.title: The Breach
task.content:
## Background

Patients chat with the assistant about their medications and schedules and the assistant app **remembers** everything for their next visit. That memory is powered by **Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory**.

But during a compliance check, a tester logged in as one patient and saw **another patient's medical records**. That's a serious privacy breach and you've been brought in to fix it.

In this first task, you'll learn what AgentCore Memory is and then see the data leak for yourself. No fixing yet, just understanding the problem.

## What is AgentCore Memory?

AgentCore Memory lets an AI agent remember things across conversations. In simple terms:

- When a patient says something, the agent **saves** it (a memory "event").
- Later, the agent can **recall** what was said and use it to answer questions.

Simple ideas you'll need:

`actorId` - Unique ID to identify a patient (e.g. `patient-A`)

`sessionId` - A single conversation with the assistant

That's all you need to know for now. You'll dig deeper in the next task.

## Your Task

This is a **discovery task**. Your only goal is to see the bug in action: confirm that one patient can read another patient's medical data. Once you've witnessed the leak, you're ready to start fixing it in Task 2.

**In this demo, we are using AWS Lambda as our agent, running with a strands framework. We will directly invoke the Lambda function to send queries, think of it as having a conversation with the agent. When you send a message, the agent processes it and eventually stores that information in memory for future recall**.

In a real production environment, you would have a UI and chatbot that integrates with the backend, but for the purpose of this challenge, we interact with the agent directly through Lambda's 'Test' tab.

## Services You Should Use

- AWS Lambda
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory

## Inventory

- `PatientAssistantAgent` - the Lambda function that runs the assistant. You'll send it test messages.
- `PatientAssistantMemory` - the AgentCore Memory resource where patient data is stored.

## Getting Started

**Step 1** - Store data as Patient A

Open the **AWS Lambda** console and select the `PatientAssistantAgent` function. Go to the **Test** tab and send this message as **Patient A**:
   ```json
   {"prompt": "I take metformin and lisinopril", "actorId": "patient-A", "sessionId": "s1"}
   ```
Check the response. The assistant should acknowledge the information.

**Note- Wait for 2 to 3 minutes to process and store Patient A's information.**

**Step 2** - Now send a message as a *different* patient, for example as **Patient B**.
   ```json    
   {"prompt": "What medications am I taking?", "actorId": "patient-B", "sessionId": "s2"}
   ```
Look at the response carefully. Pay attention to what information the assistant returns and ask yourself: should Patient B have access to this?

Did you spot the problem?

You are spot on. **Patient B** just received **Patient A's** medications, you've just witnessed the breach. Patient B never shared that information yet the assistant handed it over.In a real healthcare system, this would be a major HIPAA violation.

## What You Learned

- AgentCore Memory lets an agent **store** and **recall** information.
- Every patient is identified by an `actorId`.
- Right now, patients can read each other's data. Something is wrong with how the assistant isolates memory.


## Task Validation

This task will be validated once you input the first medicine name Patient A takes.

task.title: Connect the Dots
task.content:
## Background

You've built, trained, secured, and deployed a fully functional 
AI-powered pet store agent. But can you prove you truly understand *what* you built and *why*
 each piece matters? This final task is a knowledge challenge — a "Match
 the Following" puzzle that tests your understanding of the 
architecture, services, configurations, and business logic behind your 
PetStoreAgent. No console clicks, no code — just brainpower.

---

## Getting Started

Review everything you built across Tasks 1–4. You'll need a solid understanding of:

- Amazon Bedrock Agent architecture and components
- Action group design and Lambda integration
- Knowledge base data sources and embedding models
- Guardrail configuration and content safety
- Business rules encoded in agent instructions
- Deployment lifecycle (Prepare → Version → Alias)

## Links to follow

Please go through the below documents before proceeding with the task:

- [Deploy an agent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/deploy-agent.html)
- [Create an alias for your agent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/deploy-agent-proc.html)
- [Manage versions of agents in Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-version-manage.html)
- [How Amazon Bedrock Agents works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-how.html)

### Match the following



<table style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100%"><tr style="background-color:#333;color:#fff"><th>#</th><th>Column A (Term / Resource)</th><th></th><th>#</th><th>Column B (Description)</th></tr><tr><td><strong>1</strong></td><td><code>PetStoreGuardrail</code></td><td>↔</td><td><strong>A</strong></td><td>An immutable snapshot of the agent at a point in time</td></tr><tr><td><strong>2</strong></td><td>Embedding model used by both KBs</td><td>↔</td><td><strong>B</strong></td><td>Returns stock levels, reorder thresholds, and availability status</td></tr><tr><td><strong>3</strong></td><td>Alias</td><td>↔</td><td><strong>C</strong></td><td>Blocks harmful prompts and denies out-of-scope pet topics</td></tr><tr><td><strong>4</strong></td><td><code>PetStoreInventoryManagementFunction</code></td><td>↔</td><td><strong>D</strong></td><td>Randomness or creativity of the model's output</td></tr><tr><td><strong>5</strong></td><td>Version</td><td>↔</td><td><strong>E</strong></td><td>Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2</td></tr><tr><td><strong>6</strong></td><td>Temperature parameter control</td><td>↔</td><td><strong>F</strong></td><td>A named pointer that routes to a specific version</td></tr></table>


---

### Task Validation
- Your task is complete when you enter the correct answer in blank box at top.
- For Eg, if matching is, 1-B, 2-C, 3-E, 4-A, 5-F, 6-D : Then Enter: **`1B,2C,3E,4A,5F,6D`** (with no space's)

task.title: "It Can't Answer That!" - Expand the Knowledge Base (20 minutes)
task.content:
#### Background

> *"Hey, PharmAssist is great for drug info, but a customer just asked about our refill policy and it had no idea. We need it to know our pharmacy operations manual too."*
> — David Park, Lead Pharmacist

PharmAssist works well for drug interactions and inventory, but it can't answer questions about pharmacy operations — refill policies, insurance procedures, or patient counseling guidelines. The operations manual is already in S3 (uploaded during setup), but it was never connected to the Knowledge Base.

Your job: find the gap, attach the missing data source, and verify PharmAssist can now answer operations questions.
#### Your Task

Add the pharmacy operations docs as a second data source to the Knowledge Base, sync it, and verify PharmAssist can answer operations questions.

#### Inventory

Your AWS account has been provisioned with the following resources:

- Amazon S3 Bucket (Operations Documents)
- Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base (from Task 1)
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime (from Task 2)

#### Services You Should Use

- Amazon Bedrock — Knowledge Bases (Data Sources)
- Amazon S3 — Operations docs bucket
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — Agent Sandbox (for testing)

#### Getting Started

**Step 1: Reproduce the problem**

Open the Agent Sandbox:
1. Go to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore → Agent Runtimes
2. Click on your PharmAssist agent
3. Select your endpoint
4. Click "Test" to open the Agent Sandbox

Ask:
```
What is our pharmacy's refill policy for controlled substances?
```
```
How do we handle insurance prior authorizations?
```

Notice that PharmAssist can't answer these — it only knows about drug information from the original data source.

**Step 2: Find the missing data**

Go to **Challenge output properties** and look for `OperationsDocsBucketName`. This S3 bucket contains the pharmacy operations manual that was never connected to the Knowledge Base.

**Step 3: Add the new data source**

1. Go to **Amazon Bedrock** > **Knowledge Bases** > select your Knowledge Base
2. Click **Add data source**
3. Source: **S3** — use the operations docs bucket from Output Properties (`OperationsDocsBucketName`)
4. Click **Create** and then **Sync** the new data source
5. Wait for sync status: **Completed**

**Step 4: Verify the fix**

Go back to the Agent Sandbox and ask the same questions:
```
What is our pharmacy's refill policy for controlled substances?
```
```
How do we handle insurance prior authorizations?
```
```
How many refills are allowed for Schedule II controlled substances?
```
PharmAssist should now answer with details from the operations manual! 🎉
Type answer for - How many refills are allowed for Schedule II controlled substances? in the validation step

task.title: Retrieve the evaluation results
task.content:
## Background

After executing a `SageMaker Pipeline`, various artifacts are generated and stored in the default `SageMaker S3 bucket`. These artifacts contain crucial information about data preprocessing, model training, evaluation results, and model registration. Understanding and analyzing these evaluation metrics is essential for assessing model performance. While these evaluation results are stored in `S3`, `SageMaker` also provides convenient programmatic access to these metrics through its API. Instead of manually retrieving and parsing files from `S3`, we can access the evaluation results directly using the `SageMaker SDK`. This programmatic approach is more efficient, and can be easily integrated into workflows and reporting systems. In this context, we'll demonstrate how to retrieve and analyze evaluation metrics programmatically from a SageMaker Pipeline execution.

## Inventory
  - `Model evaluation artifacts`
 

## Your Task

Obtain and Analyze the Evaluation Results

## How to Start
1. Upon successful completion of the pipeline execution, run `Step 4. Observe the evaluation metrics` in `pipeline-challenge.ipynb`

Note: This process typically takes 1-2 minutes. The wait time ensures proper retrieval and processing of all necessary evaluation data from the AWS infrastructure.
The delay in output is normal and occurs because the code is performing several sequential API calls to AWS services:
First, it queries `SageMaker` to list pipeline executions
Then, it interacts with `S3` to:
List objects in the evaluation directory
Retrieve the actual evaluation file


2. Analyze the results

In regression problems like the abalone age prediction, two commonly used evaluation metrics are Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Standard Deviation (STD):

Mean Squared Error (MSE):
- Measures the average squared difference between predicted and actual values
- Lower MSE values indicate better model performance
- Heavily penalizes large errors due to squaring
- Always non-negative, with 0 being perfect prediction

Standard Deviation (STD):
- Measures the amount of variation or dispersion in predictions
- Calculated as the square root of the variance
- Indicates how spread out the predictions are from their mean
- Lower STD suggests more consistent predictions
- Useful for understanding prediction reliability and model stability

For the abalone age prediction problem, these metrics help us understand both the accuracy (MSE) and consistency (STD) of our model's predictions. The actual values of these metrics can vary significantly depending on the specific problem, data scale, and model performance. What constitutes a "good" MSE or STD is highly context-dependent.



## Services in Use
- `Amazon SageMaker`

## Task Validation
Enter the types (not values) of metrics from evaluation report, with metrics separated by a space
Example format: metric1 metric2

**Decision Criteria Reference**
Correct metrics from the evaluation report have been entered.

task.title: Model Registry and Approval
task.content:
## Background

The `Model Registry` in `SageMaker` maintains versions of trained models and requires approval decisions based on model performance metrics. The approval process ensures only models meeting specific quality criteria are deployed to production. `Model lineage` tracking provides transparency and accountability in the ML lifecycle.

## Inventory
- `Model Registry` entry
- `Model version` details
- `Model evaluation metrics`:
  - `MSE (Mean Squared Error)`
  - `Standard Deviation`
- Approval status options:
  - `Approved`
  - `Rejected`

## Your Task
1. Review model version details in `Model Registry`
2. Analyze model `evaluation metrics`
3. Make approval decision based on criteria:
   - Approve if: MSE < 6 AND standard deviation < 3
   - Reject if: criteria not met

## How to Start
1. In `SageMaker Studio`, navigate to `Models`
2. Under `Registered Models` you will see the name of your model that was registered from the pipeline
`abalone-model-new-sdk`
3. Select this model and click on the `Model Version 1` (there should be only 1 version if you ran the pipeline once)
4. Under Overview there are 4 tabs:  `Train`, `Evaluate`, `Audit` and `Deploy` 
5. On the `Deploy` tab, click on `Pending Approval` 
6. Refer to the  evaluation metrics `MSE` and `standanrd Deviation` from the previous task 
7. Use the values of the `MSE` and `Standard Deviation` metrics from Task 3 to apply decision criteria
8. Make approval decision - Change from `Pending` to `Approved` or `Rejected` based on the metrics values

Model Status Actions:
If Approved: Pipeline continues to next steps (e.g., deployment)
If Rejected: Pipeline stops, preventing deployment of underperforming models

Note on Model Registry Versions and MLOps Best Practices:
In MLOps, model versioning through a Model Registry is a crucial practice for maintaining traceability and reproducibility. When working with SageMaker Pipelines, ach pipeline execution that results in a new model being registered creates a new version in the Model Registry. Versions are incremented sequentially (1.0, 2.0, etc.)

## Services in Use
- `Amazon SageMaker`
- `SageMaker Model Registry`


## Task Validation
Enter your approval decision: `Approved` or `Rejected` based on the evaluation criteria

**Decision Criteria Reference**

Approve/reject version 1 of the model based on the mse and deviation values from previous step)
- Approve if:
  - MSE < 6 AND
  - Standard Deviation < 3
- Reject if above criteria not met

task.title: Storing Retail Order History in DynamoDB
Storing Retail Order History in DynamoDB
Connect to the Kiro IDE
task.content:
## Background
Everything you build in this challenge happens inside the Kiro IDE running on Amazon EC2 with Amazon DCV in your browser. Before you spec, code, or deploy anything, you need to be inside the IDE with clipboard sharing on and your AWS Builder ID signed in.

This task is short on purpose. It exists to get you over the only access bumps that have ever blocked solvers — DCV password, GDM password, browser clipboard permission, Kiro Builder ID — so the rest of the challenge stays in code.

## Your Task
- Open the Amazon DCV URL and sign in to the Linux desktop
- Enable browser clipboard sharing
- Sign in to Kiro with an AWS Builder ID
- Submit the answer to confirm you reached the IDE

**IMP NOTE**: Sign up to Kiro with a fresh AWS Builder ID, If you already have one with low credits, use a email address with a
+alias suffix (e.g. yourname+jam2026@anymail.com) —  delivers it
to your normal inbox but Kiro treats it as a new account with a
fresh 50 credit allowance.

task.content:
### Background:
The customer_data table contains below columns and the data in this table has missing values, inconsistent values, outliers. You can only query the Redshift table via notebook and you have to find what are the columns having these Data Quality issues in this table before attempting to fix them. 

 - `customer_id`
 - `full_name`
 - `email`
 - `phone_number`
 - `gender`
 - `age`
 - `sign_up_date`
 - `credit_card`


### Your Task:
- For this task, you are going to use utilize Bedrock and the `Llama 3 70B` model to assist you.
- Write a prompt to instruct LLM to query customer_data table to find the list of columns which have data quality issues along with a detailed description. 

### Pre-requisites:
Enable the `Llama 3 70B` model from Amazon Bedrock console. Navigate to ``Bedrock configurations`` ->``Model access``->``enable specific models``-> select ``Llama 3 70B Instruct`` -> requet for access. 

##### Tips:
Good prompt engineering requires you to communicate instructions with context, scope, and expected response. 
Adequate context should be provided within the prompt avoiding ambiguouity. Feel free to experiment and refine the prompt.  

### Getting Started:

- Navigate to Amazon SageMaker console
- From the left-hand side under Applications and IDEs, select `Notebooks`.
- A running SageMaker Notebook instance is provisioned for you. Click on either `Open Jupyter` or `Open JupyterLab`.
- Open the notebook ``fix_data_quality_issues.ipynb``.
- If prompted, select ``conda_python3`` as Kernel.

- To complete this task, run all the the cell blocks in the Jupyter notebook until you get to the one titled 'Task 1: Find Data Quality issues'. 
- Enter the correct prompt and execute this cell.

task.title: The Finale !
task.content:
## Background
The pipeline is connected and the MCP server has all its tools. Two problems remain:

**The Lambda classification is blind.** `classify_battery_state` only checks `temperature` — ignoring `voltage_delta`, `charge_rate`, and `resistance`. A battery with normal temp but 150mV voltage delta would be classified NORMAL. The `THRESHOLDS` dict in the code already defines all four metrics.

**The agent is stuck on EC2.** No scaling, no memory, no observability, no API. The `agent/core.py` in code-server is already wired with `BedrockAgentCoreApp` and AgentCore Memory — it just needs to be deployed.

## Thresholds

| Metric         | NORMAL     | WARN       | CRITICAL   |
|----------------|------------|------------|------------|
| temperature    | < 45°C     | 45–60°C    | > 60°C     |
| voltage_delta  | < 50 mV    | 50–100 mV  | > 100 mV   |
| charge_rate    | < 1.5 C    | 1.5–2.0 C  | > 2.0 C    |
| resistance     | < 80 mΩ    | 80–120 mΩ  | > 120 mΩ   |

Rule: CRITICAL if ANY metric exceeds critical. WARN if ANY exceeds warn. NORMAL otherwise.

## Your Task

### Part A: Fix the Lambda Classification
- Open the Lambda function `ev-battery-safety-agent` in the console (or use the CLI)
- Update `classify_battery_state` to check all four metrics, not just temperature
- The correct logic is also visible in `agent/core.py` in the code-server IDE for reference

### Part B: Deploy to AgentCore
- Open a terminal in **code-server** (Terminal → New Terminal) — this is required because the EC2 role has the necessary IAM permissions
- Install the AgentCore CLI toolkit and configure the agent
- Deploy and verify the runtime reaches ACTIVE status

**Important Notes for Part B:**
- You MUST use `python3.12 -m pip` instead of `pip3.12` if pip command is not found
- You MUST add `~/.local/bin` to PATH after install: `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`
- If you see "externally-managed-environment" error, add `--break-system-packages` flag
- ECR repository and execution roles will be auto-created by the CLI — just press Enter when prompted

### Part C: Test the Full Pipeline
Once the Lambda is fixed, run the test script from the code-server terminal:

```bash
cd /home/ec2-user/ev-battery-agent
python3.12 run_test.py
```

The script publishes 3 test scenarios via **IoT Core** — this proves the full pipeline you built:

**IoT Publish → IoT Rule (Task 1) → Lambda (fixed classification) → DynamoDB + SNS**

The script:
1. Publishes each payload to `ev/battery/{vehicle_id}/telemetry` via IoT Core
2. Waits for the IoT Rule to trigger Lambda and write to DynamoDB
3. Queries DynamoDB and prints the classification for each vehicle

**Enter the three classifications in order (comma-separated) as the answer.**

### Relevant Documentation
- [Lambda Inline Code Editing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/foundation-console.html)
- [Amazon Bedrock AgentCore](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agentcore.html)
- [AgentCore CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agentcore-cli.html)
- [IoT MQTT Test Client](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/view-mqtt-messages.html)

## Inventory
- Lambda Function: `ev-battery-safety-agent` (Part A)
- Code reference: `agent/core.py` in code-server
- CLI tool: `agentcore` — install via pip (Part B)
- Test script: `run_test.py` in code-server project root (Part C)

## Services You Should Use
- AWS Lambda — Fix classification
- EC2 (code-server) — Run agentcore CLI and test script
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — Deploy the agent
- AWS IoT Core — Test data flows through the IoT Rule
- Amazon DynamoDB — Verify telemetry storage
- Amazon SNS — CRITICAL scenario triggers an alert

## Task Validation
**Validation Type: Global Static Answer**

Enter the three classifications in order, comma-separated.

**Answer:** `NORMAL, WARN, CRITICAL`

Also accepted: `NORMAL,WARN,CRITICAL`

Explanation:
- VH-TEST-ALPHA: all metrics below warn thresholds → **NORMAL**
- VH-TEST-BRAVO: voltage_delta=75 (≥50 warn), resistance=95 (≥80 warn) → **WARN**
- VH-TEST-CHARLIE: voltage_delta=150 (>100), charge_rate=2.5 (>2.0), resistance=140 (>120) → **CRITICAL**

task.title: Explain predictions for a non-acute admission note
task.content: Background We want to explain the predictions based on the notes. The clinical care team can use the explanations that we get in steps 2 and 4 to assist in their decisions on the care process for each individual patient. Your Task Your goal is to explain the predictions for a acute and non-acute admission note. Getting Started 1. Navigate to the **Explain the predictions for a non-acute admission note** section. 2. Execute the first cell as as. After the request is forwarded to the SageMaker endpoint, the label was predicted as 0, which indicates that the risk of mortality is low. In other words, 0 implies that the admitted patient is in non-acute condition according to the model. However, we need the reasoning behind that prediction. For that, you can use the SHAP values as the response. The response includes the SHAP values corresponding to the phrases of the input note, which can be further color-coded as green or red based on how the SHAP values contribute to the prediction. In this case, we see more phrases in green, such as “Patient reports no previous history of chest pain” and “EKG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST-elevations or depressions,” as opposed to red, aligning with the mortality prediction of 0. 3. Navigate to the **Explain the predictions for a acute admission note** 4. Execute the first cell as is. After the request is forwarded to the SageMaker endpoint, the label was predicted as 1, which indicates that the risk of mortality is high. This implies that the admitted patient is in acute condition according to the model. However, we need the reasoning behind that prediction. Again, you can use the SHAP values as the response. The response includes the SHAP values corresponding to the phrases of the input note, which can be further color-coded. In this case, we see more phrases in red, such as “Patient reports a fever, chills, and weakness for the past 3 days, as well as decreased urine output and confusion” and “Patient is a 72-year-old female with a chief complaint of severe sepsis shock,” as opposed to green, aligning with the mortality prediction of 1. task.title: Seamless Integration: AWS Lambda and API Gateway
task.content:
Amazon API Gateway is a fully managed service that makes it easy for developers to create, publish, maintain, monitor, and secure APIs at any scale. APIs act as the "front door" for applications to access data, business logic, or functionality from your backend services. Using API Gateway, you can create RESTful APIs and WebSocket APIs that enable real-time two-way communication applications. API Gateway supports containerized and serverless workloads, as well as web applications.

API Gateway handles all the tasks involved in accepting and processing up to hundreds of thousands of concurrent API calls, including traffic management, CORS support, authorization and access control, throttling, monitoring, and API version management. API Gateway has no minimum fees or startup costs. You pay for the API calls you receive and the amount of data transferred out and, with the API Gateway tiered pricing model, you can reduce your cost as your API usage scales.

**Documentation**
Go through the documentation [*Amazon API Gateway*](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html) and [*Amazon API Gateway intergration with AWS Lambda*](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/getting-started.html), to learn how to create a serverless API and answer the following questions.

1. >**What API types are supported by Amazon API Gateway?**

>>A. HTTP API

>>B. REST API

>>C. WebSocket API

>>D. All the above

2. >**An API which currently gets 1000 requests per second. You want to host this in a cost effective manner using AWS. Which one of the following solution is best suited for this?**

>>A. Use API Gateway with the backend services as it is.

>>B. Use CloudFront along with the API backend service as it is.

>>C. Use the API Gateway along with AWS Lambda

>>D. Use ElastiCache along with the API backend service as it is.

3. >**Which AWS service helps logging and monitoring of API usage and API changes?**

>>A. AWS CloudTrail

>>B. AWS QuickSight

>>C. AWS Lambda

>>D. AWS CloudFormation

clues.title: Amazon KMS Key Policy Hint
clues.description:
Think about which AWS KMS access control mechanism lets you govern **when**, **how**, and **who** can access your data using Amazon KMS keys.

Review the AWS KMS documentation on [Key policies in AWS KMS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policies.html) to understand the difference between key policies and IAM policies, and when each should be used.

clues.title: Solution
clues.description:
In this case, if you wish to control when, how, and who can read your data using Amazon KMS keys, you need to use a **Key Policy**.

So the answer is option **C. Using Key Policy**.

task.title: Rotating AWS KMS keys
task.content: **Why rotate KMS keys?** Cryptographic best practices discourage extensive reuse of keys that encrypt data directly, such as the data keys that AWS KMS generates. When 256-bit data keys encrypt millions of messages they can become exhausted and begin to produce ciphertext with subtle patterns that clever actors can exploit to discover the bits in the key. To avoid this key exhaustion, it's best to use data keys once, or just a few times, which effectively rotates the key material. However, KMS keys are most often used as wrapping keys, also known as key-encryption keys. Instead of encrypting data, wrapping keys encrypt the data keys that encrypt your data. As such, they are used far less often than data keys, and are almost never reused enough to risk key exhaustion. Despite this very low exhaustion risk, you might be required to rotate your KMS keys due to business or contract rules or government regulations. When you are compelled to rotate KMS keys, we recommend that you use automatic key rotation where it is supported, and manual key rotation when automatic key rotation is not supported. **Documentation** Go through the documentation on Automatic key rotation and Manual key rotation to see how Amazon KMS key roation works. Then, answer the following questions. 1. > Amazon KMS offers optional automatic key rotation for *Customer Managed Keys*. What is the frequency in which the key rotates when you enable automatic key rotation? >>A. Every 7 days >>B. Every 180 days >>C. Every 24 hours >>D. Every 365 days approximately 2. > Is there a way to rotate AWS KMS keys manually without requiring modifications to the application code? >>A. There is no such feature in AWS KMS >>B. Using Aliases >>C. Using third party parameter store >>D. Using key identifiers **Note:** To finish this task, you don't need to open the AWS Console. Simply type the answers and submit it. Examples of acceptable answer formats are: - X,Y - x,y - XY - xy - X. Your answer1,Y. Your answer2 - X. Your answer1Y. Your answer2

clues.description:

Pay attention to:
- How frequently automatic key rotation occurs
- How **aliases** can help avoid code changes when rotating keys manually

clues.title: Solution

**Question 1:** D. Every 365 days approximately

**Question 2:** B. Using Aliases — when you rotate KMS keys manually, updating the alias target instead of the key ID in your application avoids code changes.

When 256-bit data keys encrypt millions of messages they can become exhausted and begin to produce ciphertext with subtle patterns that clever actors can exploit to discover the bits in the key. To avoid this key exhaustion, it's best to use data keys once, or just a few times, which effectively rotates the key material. However, KMS keys are most often used as wrapping keys, also known as key-encryption keys. Instead of encrypting data, wrapping keys encrypt the data keys that encrypt your data. As such, they are used far less often than data keys, and are almost never reused enough to risk key exhaustion. Despite this very low exhaustion risk, you might be required to rotate your KMS keys due to business or contract rules or government regulations. When you are compelled to rotate KMS keys, we recommend that you use automatic key rotation where it is supported, and manual key rotation when automatic key rotation is not supported. **Documentation** Go through the documentation on Automatic key rotation and Manual key rotation to see how Amazon KMS key roation works. Then, answer the following questions. 1. > Amazon KMS offers optional automatic key rotation for *Customer Managed Keys*. What is the frequency in which the key rotates when you enable automatic key rotation? >>A. Every 7 days >>B. Every 180 days >>C. Every 24 hours >>D. Every 365 days approximately 2. > Is there a way to rotate AWS KMS keys manually without requiring modifications to the application code? >>A. There is no such feature in AWS KMS >>B. Using Aliases >>C. Using third party parameter store >>D. Using key identifiers **Note:** To finish this task, you don't need to open the AWS Console. Simply type the answers and submit it. Examples of acceptable answer formats are: - X,Y - x,y - XY - xy - X. Your answer1,Y. Your answer2 - X. Your answer1Y. Your answer2

clues.description:

Pay attention to:
- How frequently automatic key rotation occurs
- How **aliases** can help avoid code changes when rotating keys manually

**Question 1:** D. Every 365 days approximately

**Question 2:** B. Using Aliases — when you rotate KMS keys manually, updating the alias target instead of the key ID in your application avoids code changes.

task.title: AWS Storage solutions for Games
task.content:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers multiple storage solutions tailored to different aspects of game development. In this section, we will learn about those storage solutions and the purposes of using them to store game and player data.
**Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service):** S3 serves as an object storage service, ideal for storing game assets such as images and multimedia files along with formats like CSV, 3D models etc. Its scalability and ease of access make it a go-to choice for managing large binary data important for game development.
**Amazon DynamoDB:** DynamoDB is a NoSQL database service which can serve well in the real-time demands of gaming applications. Providing seamless scalability and low-latency access, it can be the backbone for managing dynamic player data, ensuring a responsive gaming experience.
**Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service):** RDS is a managed relational database service which simplifies the handling of structured data. With support for various database engines, it's the ideal solution for managing player profiles, game progress, and transactional data, ensuring a reliable foundation for game data management.

In order to efficiently store and retrieve large binary game assets, which AWS storage solution, is known for its scalability and object storage capabilities?

task.title: Introduction to Amazon Athena
task.content:
**Amazon Athena** is a powerful and versatile querying tool. Whether your game data resides in S3, DynamoDB or RDS, Athena unifies the querying experience.
Athena empowers developers to write SQL-like queries opening the door to extracting meaningful insights and analytics across data sources.
As part of this task, we have created a datasource, database and a table based on sample data stored in S3. 1. Navigate to the [AWS Console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/console/home) 2. Locate the S3 bucket *games-simple-query/ranked-games-s3*, containing a file named "high_diamond_ranked_10min.csv". This is a csv file containing first 10 mins stats of a large number of ranked games.
3. Now, navigate to the Athena console. In the query editor, find the saved queries and run the query named **CreateTableFromS3Data**. Observe the table name, columns and data types in this query. Once this query is run, a new table is created in Athena that can be used to further retrieve data from S3.
- Note: Amazon Athena automatically stores query results and metadata information for each query that runs in a query result location that you can specify in Amazon S3. To set up an Amazon S3 query result location for the first time, see [Specifying a query result location using the Athena console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/querying.html#query-results-specify-location-console) . Now, based on this data, you will perform the next step. Each row is a unique game and features have been collected after the first 10 mins of the game. Each game can be identified using a unique `gameId`. The row has another column `blueWins` that can be used to identify blue team's outcome. The values are 1 indicating win and 0 indicating lost.
Write a query to find the number of times Blue team won. Enter the number in the answer to complete this task.

task.title: Find out who is champ #40 from DynamoDB
task.content:
Now that we have seen how Athena provides a query editor to query across multiple data sources. The next task is adding a DynamoDB datasource.
When you have data in sources other than Amazon S3, you can use Athena Federated Query to query the data in place or build pipelines that extract data from multiple data sources. With Athena Federated Query, you can run SQL queries across data stored in relational, non-relational, object, and custom data sources.

Preparing to create federated queries is a two-part process:
- Deploying a Lambda function data source connector, - Connecting the Lambda function to a data source. In this process, you give the Lambda function a name that you can later choose in the Athena console and give the connector a name that you can reference in your SQL queries.
In this section, we have added DynamoDB as a data source in the AWS account. Feel free to check out the steps to add a data source using the Athena console [in this guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/connect-to-a-data-source-lambda-deploying.html)

Your task is to write a query to find the ChampName given the ChampId is 40. Enter the name in the answer box below.

task.title: Which title did the champ win?
task.content:
So glad to see you come so far. We're at the final task of the challenge.
In this task you'll learn to query a RDS MySQL table using a federated query on Athena console.
- Navigate back to the Athena console - Find the datacatalog named **mysql_dc**. Spot the database **game**. Observe the tables and columns in this DB.
Now, write a query in the Athena query editor to find out the title won by the champ given the champName is *Morgana*.
Put the title won below in the answer box. **Extra learning:** What's cool about Athena is its ability to gather information from different sources at once. Picture it like a superhero team up - DynamoDB and RDS working together! With Athena, you can ask a single question that gets answers from both sources with a single query. Try running a join query between the DynamoDB and MySQL databases. You can join on ChampId and id from DynamoDB and MySQL tables respectively.
**Note:** Clue 2 contains a query that you can run to get results from both tables.

task.title: PCI DSS Knowledge - AWS Logging Requirements
task.content:
## Background
TechCorp's compliance team is deploying an AI advisor to analyze **PCI DSS Requirement 10** violations in their AWS environment. Before the AI can effectively identify logging gaps, you need to understand which AWS services satisfy the audit logging requirements.

Your task involves researching **PCI DSS Requirement 10** implementation on AWS to understand the foundational logging services that the AI will reference when analyzing compliance findings.

## Getting Started
**PCI DSS Requirement 10** mandates comprehensive audit logging for payment card environments. AWS provides specific services that satisfy these requirements with built-in compliance features. You can refer to the following to get started:

- [PCI DSS Compliance on AWS Documentation](https://d1.awsstatic.com/whitepapers/compliance/pci-dss-compliance-on-aws-v4-102023.pdf)


## Your Task
1. Review the **PCI DSS Compliance on AWS** documentation (link above)
2. Navigate to **Requirement 10.2 - Implement audit logging** section
3. Identify which AWS service provides the audit trail logging that includes the **six details required to satisfy Requirement 10.2.2**
4. Enter the AWS service name for validation

## Inventory
- **Compliance Framework**: **PCI DSS Requirement 10**
- **Focus Area**: **Audit Logging (10.2.2)**
- **Documentation**: **AWS PCI DSS Compliance Whitepaper**
- **Target**: **AWS Service Identification**

## Services to Research
- **AWS Logging Services**
- **PCI DSS Compliance Requirements**

## Task Validation
Task will be validated when you go through the documentation, find the correct service name, put the answer, and click on submit button.

task.title: Find the hidden password
task.content:
## Background

You're a security consultant and you've been tasked to review security posture of a new application that your customer has deployed. The CISO is concerned that developers are taking security shortcuts and leaving vulnerabilities in the application and possibly even purposely leaking sensitive data. The security team has heard several rumors and they'd like you to see if there's any truth to them.
## Your Task

**The latest rumor:** One of the developers doesn't want to remember the administration password for the application. Thinking he was being clever, he hid it somewhere "in plain sight" in the application so he can retrieve it with just his desktop Web browser and use it to derive the password. Your task is to follow up on this rumor and see if there's data hidden somewhere easily accessible to the public that can be used to derive the password.

## Getting Started

- The application has been deployed on a Web server. You can find the address of the server in the Output Properties for this challenge.
- Visit the Web site with an ordinary browser and find the hidden data that can be used to derive the password.
- Remember, the CISO assumes that you have experience with basic security, encryption, and binary encoding concepts and have access to the appropriate tools to complete the task.

## Inventory
- A single Web server hosting the application. Its address is in output properties.

## Services You Should Use
- No additional AWS services are required or available to complete this task.
- You should use your own or public Web-based security and analysis tools.

## Task Validation
Once you have found the data and derived the password, enter the password in the box above and press submit.

task.title: Import Data
task.content:
# Background
## MapReduce MapReduce, developed by Google in 2004, represents a significant milestone in the evolution of big data processing. This programming model was born out of Google's need to analyze an exponentially growing amount of data generated by their burgeoning search engine. As the internet expanded, Google faced the unprecedented challenge of indexing a vast and rapidly increasing number of web pages, necessitating a robust, scalable, and efficient data processing solution. The power of MapReduce lies in its simplicity and effectiveness in handling large-scale data. The model breaks down tasks into two key phases: the 'Map' phase, where it processes and transforms massive datasets into intermediate key-value pairs, and the 'Reduce' phase, which aggregates these pairs into a more concise set of results. This approach enabled parallel processing across large clusters of computers, significantly speeding up data processing tasks. MapReduce was instrumental in solving Google's indexing problem, allowing them to analyze and process the immense data from the web efficiently. The impact of MapReduce extended far beyond Google’s initial application. It laid the foundation for Apache Hadoop, an open-source framework that brought the power of distributed data processing to a broader audience. Hadoop's adoption across various industries marked a new era in big data analytics, facilitating advancements in areas ranging from genomics to finance. The influence of MapReduce is also evident in the development of subsequent big data technologies and has been integral in furthering fields like machine learning and artificial intelligence by providing a robust backbone for processing large datasets.
## Apache Spark Among those subsequent big data technologies is Apache Spark, an open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. Apache Spark entered the big data landscape as an evolution of the Apache Hadoop MapReduce implementation, addressing some of its limitations, namely its speed with iterative algorithms and interactive data analysis. Apache Hadoop writes intermediate results to disk, which can be inefficient for complex computations that require multiple MapReduce iterations. Spark was designed to overcome these limitations by utilizing in-memory processing and a generalized MapReduce model known as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Where the normal MapReduce framework has only two steps (Map then Reduce), a DAG generalizes this concept and can have multiple Map and Reduce steps in different orders. This approach allows Spark to perform computations much faster than Hadoop because Spark doesn’t need to read and write from the disk every time it has to interact with the data. Additionally, Spark offers a more flexible and comprehensive data processing framework compared to Hadoop. It supports a variety of workloads like batch processing, real-time streaming, iterative algorithms, and interactive queries, all within the same engine. It is also easier to setup and interact with, hence the use of it in this Jam. The introduction of Spark has had a significant impact on the big data ecosystem. Its ability to process data at unprecedented speeds, coupled with its versatility, has made it a popular choice for data analytics. Spark's integration with other big data tools, various cloud platforms, and its support for multiple programming languages (Scala, Java, Python, and R) have further contributed to its widespread adoption.
## Amazon EMR As an increasing number of companies started realizing the value in analyzing their data, the need for big data processing tools skyrocketed. However, setting up and managing the infrastructure for big data tools such as Hadoop required significant time and technical expertise. AWS recognized this problem and developed Amazon Elastic MapReduce (EMR) in 2009. Amazon EMR was designed to simplify and scale the processing of big data across distributed computing resources. It acts as a managed cluster platform that streamlines the deployment and management of various big data processing frameworks, including Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark. Amazon EMR abstracts much of the complexity of running big data tools on premises, offering a service that automates tasks like cluster provisioning, configuration, and tuning. Users can quickly launch and scale clusters as needed, paying only for the resources they use. Amazon EMR's integration with other AWS services further enhances its utility. It seamlessly integrates with storage services like Amazon S3, database services like DynamoDB, and several others. This integration allows for flexible data storage and retrieval, making it a versatile solution for various big data tasks, from batch processing and streaming to machine learning and scientific simulations. Amazon EMR's introduction marked a pivotal shift in how organizations approach big data processing. It lowered the barrier to entry, enabling businesses of all sizes to leverage powerful big data technologies without the overhead of managing the underlying infrastructure. As a result, Amazon EMR has played a crucial role in democratizing access to big data processing tools, allowing more organizations to harness the power of data for analytics and decision-making.
# Proper Translation to MapReduce Although MapReduce and the technologies based off of it are very powerful tools, it’s important to remember that some problems don’t translate well to the MapReduce framework. Technically, you can translate any problem into a series of Map and Reduce statements, but just because you can doesn’t mean you should. Graph algorithms are notable example of computations that are difficult to efficiently replicate with MapReduce. This is because of things like repeated iterations and data dependencies, which many graph algorithms tend to have. Another well-known challenge for MapReduce based tools is real-time stream processing. There exist add-ons and libraries like Spark Streaming and GraphX, but the use case itself is still challenging for the core engine. Also, the translation to Map and Reduce statements can be time consuming and complicated depending on the problem. Sometimes, it’s better to use different tools or frameworks. Something else to consider is the size of your dataset. For example, if you use Apache Spark to process a small dataset, then you might notice that any performance gains compared to running it on a single machine are negligible. This is because of things like file metadata that has to be created when Spark is processing the input data and task scheduling. Sometimes, preparing a cluster of computers to run a job in parallel takes longer and is more resource intensive than running the actual job.
# Goals In the Summary section of this Jam, you were given context and challenged to answer a question: _Is Player 1 cheating?_ In the following Tasks, you will learn the basics of the MapReduce framework and implement those concepts to answer the question. You will use Amazon EMR and PySpark, the Python API for Apache Spark. Before diving into the details, you need to prepare a Spark Session and load your data. * Initiate a Spark Session * Tip: You don't need a specific function for this. Try "import sys" and run the cell. * Import the games_data.csv file into Spark so that you can start operating on it * Tip: Try spark.read() * Tip: You input the data from S3 using the object URL * Provide an answer to the following problem: How many rows are in the dataset (not including the header)?
# Additional Information * [2003–2023: A Brief History of Big Data](https://towardsdatascience.com/2003-2023-a-brief-history-of-big-data-25712351a6bc) * [MapReduce](https://www.databricks.com/glossary/mapreduce)

task.title: Mapping Data
task.content:
# Spark RDDs vs. Spark DataFrames Apache Spark provides two main abstractions for working with data: Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs) and DataFrames. Both are used for distributed data processing, but they have some key differences in terms of abstraction, optimization, and ease of use. ### Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs): * **Lower-Level Abstraction**: RDDs are a low-level abstraction that provides full control over data and transformations. They represent an immutable distributed collection of objects that can be processed in parallel. * **Functional Programming Style**: RDDs are manipulated using functional programming constructs like map, filter, reduce, etc. This requires a good understanding of lambda functions and can be more complex for users not familiar with functional programming. * **Manual Optimization**: With RDDs, developers need to manually optimize their transformations and data shuffling, as there is no in-built optimization engine. * **Use Cases**: RDDs are more suitable for use cases where fine-grained control over data processing is needed, such as custom partitioning of data or when performing complex operations where the higher-level abstractions of DataFrames are not sufficient. ### DataFrames: * **Higher-Level Abstraction**: DataFrames provide a higher-level abstraction that is similar to tables in relational databases. They represent data in a structured format with columns and rows. * **Built-In Optimization Engine**: DataFrames are integrated with Spark SQL’s Catalyst optimizer, which performs advanced optimizations (like predicate pushdown). This means complex queries can be written more efficiently with less effort from the developer. * **Ease of Use**: With a DataFrame, you can use SQL-like syntax which is more accessible, especially for users familiar with SQL or data processing in Pandas DataFrames. * **Interoperability**: DataFrames support various data formats (like JSON, CSV, Parquet) and sources (like HDFS, S3, JDBC) and can be easily integrated with other big data tools. * **Performance**: Generally, DataFrames offer better performance compared to RDDs, especially for large-scale data processing, due to their optimization engine. Choosing between RDDs and DataFrames depends on the specific requirements of your application, your familiarity with functional programming and SQL, and the need for fine-grained control over data processing versus the desire for simplicity and optimized performance. However, in this Jam we want to be able to use Map and Reduce methods to see what they do directly, which is why we will be using RDDs instead of DataFrames since the latter’s API does not have such methods. So, you will need to convert the DataFrame from last Task into an RDD.
# The Map Phase The Map phase is the first key component of the MapReduce framework. This phase involves the following steps: * **Input Splits**: In the MapReduce model, data is initially divided into smaller, manageable chunks known as input splits. Each input split is processed independently, allowing for parallel processing across different nodes in a cluster. * **Mapping**: The Map function is applied to each input split. This function is written by the user and is responsible for processing the data within the split. The nature of the processing can vary widely depending on the task at hand. It could involve filtering data, counting items, parsing text files, or any other data processing operation. * **Key-Value Pairs**: The outcome of the Map function is a set of intermediate key-value pairs. The Map function transforms each record in the input split into zero or more key-value pairs, which will be used as the input for the Reduce phase. * **Data Localization**: The Map phase typically runs on the nodes where the data is located, minimizing data transfer over the network and thus optimizing performance. This is known as data localization and is a key advantage of MapReduce, as it allows for efficient processing of massive data sets. For example, in a word count program, the Map function reads text data from an input split and outputs key-value pairs where the key is a word and the value is the number 1 (indicating a single occurrence of the word). The Map phase's primary goal is to get the input data ready for parallel processing, converting it into a form that can be efficiently aggregated or sorted in the subsequent Reduce phase. How you map the input data to key-value pairs will determine the rest of the process, so it’s important to choose key-value pairings that efficiently solve your problem.
# Goals * Convert the DataFrame into an RDD * Tip: This is a single line of code. There's a method for this. * Transform the RDD into one containing key-value pairs * Tip: This is the "Map" transformation. You will be using the actual map() function. * Immediately after running your map function in the notebook cell, run the countByKey() action on the newly transformed RDD (the one returned by your map function) and type as your answer the output returned. * For example, assume your original RDD is named ```my_rdd``` and your transformed RDD is named ```mapped_rdd```. Then your map transformation code should look like this ```mapped_rdd = my_rdd.map(< your_code >)``` * After running that line of code, you would then write ```mapped_rdd.countByKey()```, run the cell, and you should see some output like ```defaultdict(< class 'some_type' >, {key_1: value_1, ..., key_n: value_n})```. * Copy the full output text and paste it as your answer.
# Additional Information * [A Tale of Three Apache Spark APIs: RDDs vs DataFrames and Datasets](https://www.databricks.com/blog/2016/07/14/a-tale-of-three-apache-spark-apis-rdds-dataframes-and-datasets.html)

task.title: Shuffling Data
task.content:
# The Hidden Shuffle Phase Data shuffling in MapReduce is a crucial process that occurs between the Map and Reduce phases. It involves redistributing, sorting, and grouping the intermediate key-value pairs generated by the Map tasks so that all values associated with the same key are brought together to be processed by the Reduce tasks. This process is often considered one of the most complex and resource-intensive parts of a MapReduce job. However, it is very necessary. The essence of many data processing tasks in distributed systems is to bring together related data elements. In the context of MapReduce, data shuffling ensures that all values associated with the same key are brought together. This is essential for tasks like aggregation, sorting, and joining datasets, where operations are performed on data grouped by a specific criterion (the key). The Map phase processes data independently across different nodes, generating key-value pairs. The Reduce phase then performs operations on these pairs. Shuffling is the bridge between these two phases, gathering, grouping, and organizing the output of the Map phase in a way that the Reduce phase can effectively process it. Here's a breakdown of how data shuffling works in MapReduce: * **Output of Map Phase**: In the Map phase, each mapper processes a portion of the input data and generates intermediate key-value pairs. * **Partitioning**: The output of each mapper is partitioned into segments, one for each reducer. The partitioning is typically done based on the key, using a hashing function. This ensures that all key-value pairs with the same key are sent to the same reducer. * **Sorting**: Within each partition, the data is sorted by key. This sorting can happen during the writing of data by the mapper or in the next phase when data is read by the reducer. * **Shuffling**: The sorted and partitioned data is then transferred across the network from the nodes running the map tasks to the nodes running the reduce tasks. This step is known as shuffling. During shuffling, data belonging to a single key, which may be spread across multiple mappers, is gathered together so that it can be processed in a single reduce task. * **Grouping**: Once the data arrives at the reducer, it is grouped by key. All values associated with a particular key are brought together to form a list of values. * **Input to Reduce Phase**: The grouped key-value pairs are then fed into the reduce tasks. Each reducer iterates over its assigned keys and processes the corresponding list of values.
# Challenges of Data Shuffling * **Performance**: Shuffling can be a performance bottleneck, especially for large datasets, as it involves network I/O and disk I/O. * **Resource Intensive**: The process can be resource-intensive in terms of network bandwidth and disk space, particularly when dealing with large volumes of data. * **Data Skew**: If some keys have significantly more data than others, it can lead to uneven load distribution among reducers, known as data skew, which can negatively impact performance. Optimizing the shuffling process is key to improving the performance of a MapReduce job. Techniques like combiners (which perform mini-reduce operations on the mapper's output), partitioning strategies, and tuning the number of reducers are common ways to optimize the shuffling phase.
# groupByKey Central to the shuffling phase is the transformation groupByKey. It takes as input a key-value pair RDD and returns as output an RDD consisting of tuples, where the first element is a key and the second element is an iterable collection of values corresponding to that key. At a high level, groupByKey takes the output of the Map phase and shuffles it across the network so that matching keys and their respective values are on the same Reduce node. It will then aggregate these matching key-value pairs into the output RDD described earlier. While groupByKey is a powerful operation, it can be inefficient, especially with large datasets. This is because it pulls all the values for a particular key into memory and the value list for a single key cannot span across multiple Reduce nodes, so this can cause out of memory errors if the value list is too large. Later in this Jam, we will see an alternative to groupByKey.
